# One Word a Page

The dictionary cost a dollar at the estate sale, wedged between a bread machine nobody wanted and a box of Christmas candles. Webster's Collegiate, ninth edition, spine cracked to white. I bought it because my old dictionary had drowned in a basement flood and I had been making do with the internet, which hands you a word the way a vending machine hands you a candy bar — instantly, and without any sense that a word has neighbors, or a history, or a body.

It wasn't until I got home that I found the underlines.

Someone had gone through this dictionary the way a child goes through a coloring book. On the first page, a clean stroke beneath *abandon*. On the second, *abate*. Not every page. Not random pages either, or so it seemed at first. One word, sometimes two, then a stretch of ten or fifty pages in silence. I sat on the floor in the window light and turned the pages like a person dealing out a fortune.

*Abandon. Abate. Aberrant. Abide.*

I want to tell you I didn't make a list. I made a list.

The sale had been for a house on Maple Street, the kind with a screened porch and a flag holder by the door. The woman running the cash box said the owner had lived there forty years. A teacher, maybe. A widow. She didn't know much. "She kept to herself," the woman said, which is what people say when they mean they never asked.

From the A's I copied: *after, alone, amber, anchor, answer, archipelago, attend, August, awake.*

I looked the sale up that night and found the obituary. Her name was Ruth Voss. Born 1931. Taught fourth grade for thirty-one years. Husband dead in 1988. Garden, church, a nephew in Ohio. The obituary did not mention words. Most obituaries don't. They list the weather of a life without ever saying what fell.

The B's: *because, begin, believe, beneath, bird, bloom, breathe, bright.* The C's: *candle, carry, certain, chase, clear, close, cloud, come.* I noticed the words leaning one direction — verbs of continuing, nouns of weather and light. A person could live inside a list like that. A person could be trying to.

I started writing a story about her. In my story she left a marriage in 1974 and drove to the ocean with a dictionary on the passenger seat. I gave her a blue coat. Then I realized I had given her my blue coat, and I stopped writing the story. That is the trouble with any trace of a stranger. You read it like a mirror and call it a biography.

A friend of mine said, people underline in books, old people especially, it doesn't mean a thing. Maybe she just liked the drag of the pen. But the lines were confident — one stroke, no going back over, the ballpoint never hesitating on the fiber. And it was the same pen the whole way through, blue, until the last quarter of the book, where the ink goes black and the lines begin to wobble. The hand was older. Or tired. Or both.

I tried to imagine the nights. A kitchen table. A lamp with a pull chain. She would not have been reading for information — you don't read a dictionary for information. You read it the way you walk a property line, to see what's yours, to see what holds. Maybe it was a game she played with a grandchild who didn't exist. Maybe it was prayer. Some people close their eyes and put a finger on a page and believe the finger is guided. The underlines were too many for that, and too patient. This was not one answer sought. This was a practice.

You cannot hurry a book you've promised to meet one word at a time. That is the opposite of skimming. Skimming is how we read now, and I don't except myself. We take the vending-machine word and go. She had chosen the other thing: the whole field of the page, and one word allowed to survive it. Every page a small field. Every underline a decision about what matters. It must have changed her. A discipline like that always does. It's the grandmother shelling peas on the porch — the point was never the peas.

In the S's the wobbling got worse. *Stay. Still. Sure.* Then a long pause — forty pages of nothing — and then, in a black, uncertain line, *remain.*

The T's: *tender, threshold, tonight, trace, true.* The W's: *wait, want, weather, window.* Then almost nothing. The X's and Y's went by clean. On the last page of the dictionary, among the z's — *zeal, zenith, zinc, zither, zone* — no mark at all.

The last underlined word, two pages earlier, was *again.*

I sat with that for a while. *Again* is a word that only works if there is a next time. It is a word that does not close a book. She could have underlined *end.* She owned the pen. She chose *again.*

I started my own underlining around the G's. Not to imitate her. All right — to imitate her. It changed the reading within a week. I slowed down. I began to see pages as fields instead of corridors. I began to fail at it, too — to underline three words, then four, then to catch myself hoarding, and to put the pen down. One word a page is a fast way to find out what you actually want. Most of us want everything. She didn't. Or she trained herself not to.

I don't know what I'll do at the last page. Leave it clean, probably. Some words should arrive unchosen, the way mornings do.

But I copied her list out fair, all of it, and pinned it above my desk, and I will tell you the strangest thing. I cannot read it as hers anymore. I read it and it is my voice saying the words. *After, alone, amber, again.* Whatever she was doing at that kitchen table for all those years, it worked. The words got out.

**One Word a Page**

The dictionary cost a dollar at the estate sale, wedged between a bread machine nobody wanted and a box of Christmas candles. Webster's Collegiate, ninth edition, spine cracked to white. I bought it because my old dictionary had drowned in a basement flood and I had been making do with the internet, which hands you a word the way a vending machine hands you a candy bar — instantly, and without any sense that a word has neighbors, or a history, or a body.

It wasn't until I got home that I found the underlines.

Someone had gone through this dictionary the way a child goes through a coloring book. On the first page, a clean stroke beneath *abandon*. On the second, *abate*. Not every page. Not random pages either, or so it seemed at first. One word, sometimes two, then a stretch of ten or fifty pages in silence. I sat on the floor in the window light and turned the pages like a person dealing out a fortune.

*Abandon. Abate. Aberrant. Abide.*

I want to tell you I didn't make a list. I made a list.

The sale had been for a house on Maple Street, the kind with a screened porch and a flag holder by the door. The woman running the cash box said the owner had lived there forty years. A teacher, maybe. A widow. She didn't know much. "She kept to herself," the woman said, which is what people say when they mean they never asked.

From the A's I copied: *after, alone, amber, anchor, answer, archipelago, attend, August, awake.*

I looked the sale up that night and found the obituary. Her name was Ruth Voss. Born 1931. Taught fourth grade for thirty-one years. Husband dead in 1988. Garden, church, a nephew in Ohio. The obituary did not mention words. Most obituaries don't. They list the weather of a life without ever saying what fell.

The B's: *because, begin, believe, beneath, bird, bloom, breathe, bright.* The C's: *candle, carry, certain, chase, clear, close, cloud, come.* I noticed the words leaning one direction — verbs of continuing, nouns of weather and light. A person could live inside a list like that. A person could be trying to.

I started writing a story about her. In my story she left a marriage in 1974 and drove to the ocean with a dictionary on the passenger seat. I gave her a blue coat. Then I realized I had given her my blue coat, and I stopped writing the story. That is the trouble with any trace of a stranger. You read it like a mirror and call it a biography.

A friend of mine said, people underline in books, old people especially, it doesn't mean a thing. Maybe she just liked the drag of the pen. But the lines were confident — one stroke, no going back over, the ballpoint never hesitating on the fiber. And it was the same pen the whole way through, blue, until the last quarter of the book, where the ink goes black and the lines begin to wobble. The hand was older. Or tired. Or both.

I tried to imagine the nights. A kitchen table. A lamp with a pull chain. She wouldn't have been reading for information — you don't read a dictionary for information. You read it the way you walk a property line, to see what's yours, to see what holds. Maybe it was a game she played with a grandchild who didn't exist. Maybe it was prayer. Some people close their eyes and put a finger on a page and believe the finger is guided. The underlines were too many for that, and too patient. This was not one answer. This was a practice.

You cannot hurry a book you've promised to meet one word at a time. That's the opposite of skimming. Skimming is how we read now, and I don't except myself. We take the vending-machine word and go. She had chosen the other thing: the whole field of the page, and one word allowed to survive it. Every page a small field. Every underline a decision about what matters. It must have changed her. A discipline like that always does. It's the grandmother shelling peas on the porch — the point was never the peas.

In the S's the wobbling got worse. *Stay. Still. Sure.* Then a long pause — forty pages of nothing — and then, in a black, uncertain line, *remain.*

The T's: *tender, threshold, tonight, trace, true.* The W's: *wait, want, weather, window.* Then almost nothing. The X's and Y's went by clean. On the last page of the dictionary, among the z's — *zeal, zenith, zinc, zither, zone* — no mark at all.

The last underlined word, two pages earlier, was *again.*

I sat with that for a while. *Again* is a word that only works if there's a next time. It's a word that doesn't close a book. She could have underlined *end.* She owned the pen. She chose *again.*

I started my own underlining around the G's. Not to imitate her. All right — to imitate her. It changed the reading within a week. I slowed down. I began to see pages as fields instead of corridors. I began to fail at it, too — to underline three words, then four, then to catch myself hoarding, and to put the pen down. One word a page is a fast way to find out what you actually want. Most of us want everything. She didn't. Or she trained herself not to.

I don't know what I'll do at the last page. Leave it clean, probably. Some words should arrive unchosen, the way mornings do.

But I copied her list out fair, all of it, and pinned it above my desk, and I'll tell you the strangest thing. I cannot read it as hers anymore. I read it and it is my voice saying the words. *After, alone, amber, again.* Whatever she was doing in that kitchen for all those years, it works. The words got out.
